nameStory: This lichen gets its vivid name from the bumpy, blister-like structures that cover its surface, resembling tiny pustules or raised spots. The word 'crust' describes how it forms a thin, crusty layer directly on tree bark, spreading outward like a natural coating.
description: Pustule Crust Lichen is a crusty lichen that forms whitish to pale gray patches on tree bark, covered with distinctive raised bumps. These bumps, called soralia, give the lichen its characteristic pustule-like appearance. The patches can spread to cover several inches of bark surface, creating an almost warty texture that's easily spotted once you know what to look for. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together: a fungus and an algae.

idTips.label: Pustule-like bumps
idTips.description: Surface covered with small, raised, wart-like bumps that feel rough to the touch and won't rub off easily

idTips.label: Crusty base
idTips.description: Forms a thin, tightly attached crust on bark that can't be peeled off like paper - it's fused to the surface

idTips.label: Whitish-gray color
idTips.description: Overall pale coloring ranges from chalky white to light gray, sometimes with a slightly greenish tint when moist

idTips.label: Bark-dwelling
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on tree bark, never on rocks or soil, preferring smooth-barked trees

idTips.label: Powdery soralia
idTips.description: The raised bumps often split open to reveal powdery, flour-like reproductive structures inside

habitat: Look for Pustule Crust Lichen on the bark of hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, particularly on maples, oaks, and birches. It prefers trees with relatively smooth bark in partially shaded woodland areas from sea level to mid-elevations. You're most likely to spot it in mature forests where the air quality is good, as lichens are sensitive to pollution.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after winter moisture has cleaned the bark surface, making the whitish patches stand out clearly against dark tree bark.
seasonality.summer: May appear slightly less prominent during dry periods, but the distinctive pustule-like bumps remain clearly visible and are actually easier to feel.
seasonality.fall: Excellent time for observation as falling leaves expose more bark surface, and autumn moisture keeps the lichen looking fresh and well-defined.
seasonality.winter: Still clearly visible on bare trees, though snow and ice may temporarily obscure lower patches on trunks.

funFact: Despite looking like a skin condition, this lichen is actually an incredibly slow-growing partnership that can live for centuries - some patches you see today may have been starting to form when your great-grandparents were children!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other whitish crusty lichens, but the distinctive raised pustule-like bumps set it apart from smoother species. Remember: if it looks like bark with chicken pox, you've probably found Pustule Crust Lichen!
compareHints: Unlike the bitter wart lichen which has a more uniformly bumpy surface, Pustule Crust Lichen has more pronounced, blister-like raised areas. Powdered Wart Lichen tends to be more powdery overall and less distinctly pustular. The pustules on this species are typically larger and more prominent than those found on other members of the fluff-wart lichen group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bitter wart lichen differs from its close relative pustule crust lichen by having more pronounced, irregular warts rather than neat pustule-like bumps.
